newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia asks Castro to intervene in hostage case.
newsitem.headline: Colombia asks Castro to intervene in hostage case.

text.p: Colombia has asked Cuban President Fidel Castro to use his influence over its Marxist-led guerrilla groups to help win the release of 60 soldiers taken prisoner more than three months ago in southern Colombia.
Foreign Minister Maria Emma Mejia, in Havana for a Caribbean development conference, said she personally asked Castro to intervene on the soldiers' behalf at a dinner on Thursday night.
"I think the Cuban president ... is interested in making this humanitarian gesture," Mejia said in an interview with the Caracol radio station.
"I'm confident that this is going to happen," she added, when asked if Castro had committed himself to efforts to win the soldiers' freedom.

The soldiers were taken prisoner on Aug. 30 when Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) rebels overran a military base in a remote, jungle-covered area of southwestern Putumayo province. Government officials and the FARC have so far been unable to agree on terms for their release.
The FARC, Colombia's oldest and largest guerrilla group, was founded as a Marxist, pro-Soviet group in 1964.

Castro was credited last June with winning the release of former President Cesar Gaviria's younger brother after his abduction by a radical lefitst group called Dignity for Colombia. The bearded Cuban leader, whose island nation is the last bastion of communism in the Western hemisphere, is believed to wield heavy influence over the FARC and National Liberation Army, Colombia's second-largest rebel group.
